tips.title: Three numbers carry most questions
tips.body: **A is 65**, **a is 97**, **0 is 48**. Each group runs in sequence from there, so any letter or digit can be worked out by counting on. The exam gives you a table, but knowing these saves looking things up.

tips.title: Count on from the start of the group
tips.body: For any letter, take its position in the alphabet and add. **F** is the 6th letter, so its code is 65 + 5 = **70**. Count from **0**, not 1 — that off-by-one is an easy slip.

tips.title: The character "7" is not the number 7
tips.body: The digit characters start at **48**, so `'7'` has the code **55**. This is why a program has to convert a typed digit before doing arithmetic with it, and why `'2' + '2'` does not give 4.

tips.title: Upper and lower case differ by 32
tips.body: **a (97) − A (65) = 32**, and the same gap holds for every letter. So if a code you have worked out is 32 away from the answer you expected, you have the wrong case.

tips.title: Unicode matches ASCII up to 127
tips.body: The first **128** Unicode codes are **identical** to ASCII. That is why ASCII text keeps its codes in Unicode, and it is the point to make when asked about the advantages of Unicode.

why.matters:
There is no such thing as the letter A inside a computer. There is a **number** that everybody has agreed means A, and a character set is that agreement written down.

Which makes the whole topic a lesson in what a standard is for. Two programs can only exchange text if they use the same table, and every piece of mojibake you have ever seen — the black diamonds, the Â before a pound sign — is two programs disagreeing about which table this file was written with.

examples.title: Why "a" is 32 more than "A"
examples.body:
In ASCII, **A** is 65 and **a** is 97. Every capital letter is exactly **32** less than its lower-case version, because the codes were laid out in two runs on purpose.

That is why changing case is arithmetic rather than a lookup: add 32 to go down, subtract 32 to go up. The same design lets a program compare two letters of the same case just by comparing their codes, and check whether a character is a digit by asking whether its code lies between the codes for 0 and 9.

visual.alt: A table of ASCII codes showing that A is sixty-five and B sixty-six, while a is ninety-seven and b ninety-eight, so each lower-case letter is thirty-two more than its capital

examples.title: Why seven bits was not enough
examples.body:
ASCII uses **7 bits**, which gives **128** codes. That is ample for the English alphabet twice over, the digits, punctuation and some control codes — and hopeless for a world with Greek, Arabic, Chinese and emoji.

**Unicode** was the answer: far more bits, so far more characters, and room to keep adding. The decision that made it work was deciding that its first **128** codes would be **exactly ASCII's**. So every ASCII character kept its code, and text written before Unicode did not need renumbering.

props.caption: Codes available in ASCII and in Unicode

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion comparing the number of codes available: one hundred and twenty-eight in seven-bit ASCII against one million one hundred and fourteen thousand one hundred and twelve in the Unicode code space, so the ASCII bar is too small to see

examples.title: Why a file opened in the wrong program shows nonsense
examples.body:
Text on disk is only numbers. Nothing in the file says which agreement those numbers were written under, so a program opening it has to **assume** one — and if it assumes wrongly, any character whose code the two tables disagree on comes out as the wrong symbol.

Below 128 the assumption rarely matters, because Unicode agrees with ASCII there. Above it the tables disagree, which is exactly where accented letters, currency symbols and everything non-English live. That is why the mangled characters in an email are almost never the plain English words.

visual.alt: A table comparing ASCII and Unicode: the codes agree up to one hundred and twenty-seven, and above that ASCII has nothing defined while Unicode continues, which is where a file read with the wrong assumption goes wrong

steps.title: Character sets
steps.body:
**A computer stores everything as binary, including text.** So there has to be an agreed answer to the question: which bit pattern means which character?

**A character set is that agreement** — a list of the characters a system can use, each paired with a unique binary code. Without one, a file saved on one machine would be meaningless on another, because nothing would say what the patterns stood for.

**A character includes more than letters.** Digits, punctuation, the space, and **control characters** such as carriage return all have codes of their own.

**ASCII** — the American Standard Code for Information Interchange — is the older of the two the specification names. It is a **7-bit** code, so it has $2^7 = $ **128** characters, numbered **0 to 127**. That is enough for the English alphabet in both cases, the ten digits, punctuation and the control characters, and no more.

**128 is a small number.** It leaves no room for accented letters such as é, for Greek or Arabic or Chinese, or for the mathematical symbols and emoji people now expect. ASCII was designed for English on American equipment in the 1960s, and it fits that job exactly and nothing beyond it.

check.prompt: How many different characters can 7-bit ASCII represent?
check.solution: Seven bits give $2^7 = $ **128** patterns, so 128 characters with codes running 0 to 127.

steps.title: Codes run in sequence
steps.body:
**Character codes are grouped, and each group runs in order.** This is stated in the specification, and it is what makes the arithmetic questions possible.

| Group | First | Last |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capital letters | **A = 65** | Z = 90 |
| Lower case letters | **a = 97** | z = 122 |
| Digits | **0 = 48** | 9 = 57 |

**So one code per group gives you the rest.** If A is 65, then B is 66, C is 67, and any letter is 65 plus its position in the alphabet **counting from 0**.

**Count from zero.** A is 0 places along, not 1. F is the 6th letter, which is **5** places along, so 65 + 5 = **70**. Counting from 1 gives 71, and that off-by-one is easy to make.

**Upper and lower case are exactly 32 apart**, since 97 − 65 = 32. The gap is the same for every letter, so converting case is just adding or subtracting 32.

**The digit characters are not the numbers they show.** `'7'` has the code **55** (48 + 7), not 7. A program that reads a typed digit gets the **character**, and must convert it before doing arithmetic — which is why joining `'2'` and `'2'` gives `'22'` rather than 4.

steps.title: Unicode
steps.body:
**Unicode exists because 128 characters are nowhere near enough.**

**Its purpose** is to give **every character in every writing system** its own unique code — Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew, Chinese, Japanese, and the mathematical symbols, currency signs and emoji besides.

**It does this by using more bits per character.** ASCII has 7 bits and so 128 codes; Unicode uses more, which is what buys the room for over a hundred thousand characters.

**Its advantages over ASCII:**

- It can represent **far more characters** — every alphabet, not just the English one.
- Text in **any language** can be stored and exchanged, including several languages in one document.
- It is a **single worldwide standard**, so a file opens the same way everywhere. Before it there were many incompatible extensions of ASCII, and text moved between countries turned to nonsense.
- **The first 128 codes are identical to ASCII**, so every ASCII character keeps the same code in Unicode, and ASCII text did not need renumbering.

**Its disadvantage is size.** More bits per character means **larger files** for the same text, which is why plain English text in Unicode can take more space than the same text in ASCII.

**That backwards compatibility is the clever part.** Unicode could have renumbered everything and been tidier. Keeping ASCII's codes for the first 128 characters meant every ASCII character kept its code, so existing text did not have to be renumbered.

You do **not** need to know about UTF-8, UTF-16 or any other version of Unicode.

check.prompt: What is the main advantage of Unicode over ASCII?
options: It can represent characters from all writing systems, not just English
It uses fewer bits per character, so files are smaller
It stores text without needing a character set at all
It is faster for a computer to process than ASCII
check.solution: Unicode covers **every alphabet and symbol**, which 128 ASCII codes cannot. It uses **more** bits per character, so files are **larger** — that is the trade-off, not a benefit.

2. How many characters does 7-bit ASCII have, and what are the lowest and highest codes?

**Part B.**

Use A = 65, a = 97 and 0 = 48.

4. Give the code for the letter D.

**Part C.**

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Count from zero.** A is 65 and is **0** places along, so the 6th letter F is 65 + **5** = 70. Counting from 1 gives 71. It is an easy off-by-one to make.

**Check the case before you start.** Capitals begin at 65 and lower case at 97. If your answer is exactly **32** away from what you expected, you have used the wrong group.

**Keep the character and the value apart.** `'7'` is code **55**, not 7. This is not a technicality — it is why a program must convert input before doing arithmetic, and why `'2' + '2'` gives `'22'`. Saying so shows you understand what the code is for.

**Give the purpose of Unicode as coverage, not size.** It exists so that **every writing system** has its own codes. Answering that it is "bigger" describes the mechanism and misses what the question asks.

**Do not claim Unicode saves space.** It uses **more** bits per character, so the same English text takes **more** room than in ASCII. That is Unicode's one real disadvantage, and naming it makes the comparison complete.

**Make the backwards-compatibility point.** The first **128** Unicode codes are identical to ASCII, so every ASCII character keeps its code and ASCII text did not need renumbering. That is a better answer than simply listing that it has more characters.

**Remember that "character" is broader than "letter".** Punctuation, the space, and control characters such as carriage return all occupy codes. A question asking how many characters a set holds is counting all of them.

**You do not need UTF-8 or UTF-16.** The specification says so explicitly, so do not spend an answer on them.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **character set** pairs every usable character with a **unique binary code**.
- Without one, a file would be meaningless on another machine.
- Characters include **punctuation, the space and control characters**, not just letters.
- **ASCII is 7-bit**: $2^7 = $ **128** characters, codes **0 to 127**.
- Codes are **grouped and run in sequence**.
- **A = 65**, **a = 97**, **character 0 = 48**.
- Count places from **0**: F is 65 + 5 = **70**.
- Upper and lower case differ by **32**.
- The character `'7'` is code **55**, not 7.
- **Unicode's purpose** is a code for **every character in every writing system**.
- It uses **more bits**, giving over a hundred thousand characters.
- Advantages: all alphabets, any language, one worldwide standard.
- Its first **128** codes are **identical to ASCII**, so ASCII text keeps its codes.
- Its disadvantage is **larger files** for the same text.
- **UTF-8 and UTF-16 are not required.**

questions.prompt: What is a character set?
options: A font that sets how each character is drawn on screen
The keys and symbols printed on a computer keyboard
A code that scrambles text so only some can read it
A list of characters, each with a unique binary code
questions.solution: A **character set** is the agreed list of characters a system can use, each paired with a **unique binary code**, so that a stored pattern can be read back as the right character. A font only decides how a character looks, a keyboard is one way of typing them, and scrambling text is encryption.

markScheme.description: a list of characters each with a unique binary code

questions.prompt: How many different characters can 7-bit ASCII represent?
questions.solution: $2^7 = $ **128** characters, with codes running 0 to 127.

questions.prompt: In ASCII the code for A is 65. What is the code for D?
questions.solution: D is the 4th letter, so **3** places on from A. $65 + 3 = $ **68**.

questions.prompt: Which of these has its own character code in ASCII?
options: A paragraph of text
The number 300
A whole word
The space
questions.solution: The **space** is a character with its own code, as are punctuation marks and control characters. A code represents **one character**, never a word or a number larger than the set.

questions.prompt: In ASCII the code for a is 97. What is the code for q?
questions.solution: q is the 17th letter, so **16** places on from a. $97 + 16 = $ **113**.

questions.prompt: In ASCII the code for the character 0 is 48. What is the code for the character 5?
questions.solution: The digits run in sequence from 48, so $48 + 5 = $ **53**. That is the code for the **character** 5, not the value 5.

questions.prompt: By how much do the ASCII codes for a capital letter and the matching lower case letter differ?
questions.solution: Capitals start at 65 and lower case at 97, so the gap is $97 - 65 = $ **32**, and it is the same for every letter.

questions.prompt: A character has the ASCII code 84. Given that A is 65, which character is it?
questions.solution: $84 - 65 = 19$, so it is 19 places on from A. Counting from A as 0, that is the 20th capital letter: **T**.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of Unicode?
options: To replace binary storage of text with something faster
To store text using fewer bits than ASCII does
To give every character in every writing system a unique code
To encrypt text so that it cannot be read without a key
questions.solution: Unicode exists so that **every writing system** — every alphabet, plus symbols and emoji — has its own unique code. It uses **more** bits than ASCII, not fewer, and it has nothing to do with encryption.

markScheme.description: a unique code for every writing system

questions.prompt: Up to which code number does Unicode use the same codes as ASCII?
questions.solution: The first **128** codes, numbered **0 to 127**, are identical in both. So every ASCII character keeps the same code in Unicode.

questions.prompt: A student writes that Unicode is better than ASCII because it produces smaller files. Why is this wrong?
options: Unicode files are exactly the same size as ASCII files
File size depends only on the number of characters, not the encoding
Unicode uses more bits per character, so files are larger
Unicode does not store text in files at all
questions.solution: The extra characters are bought with **more bits each**, so the same English text takes **more** space in Unicode than in ASCII. Larger files are Unicode's one genuine disadvantage, and a full comparison names it.

markScheme.description: more bits per character, so larger files

questions.prompt: Why did Unicode keep ASCII's codes for its first 128 characters?
options: Because those 128 codes cannot be changed by any standard
So ASCII text would not need converting to new codes
To make Unicode files smaller than they would otherwise be
Because ASCII characters are used more often than others
questions.solution: Renumbering would have been tidier, but then **every piece of ASCII text** would have needed new codes. Keeping the ASCII codes meant every ASCII character kept the same code in Unicode, so existing text did not need renumbering.

markScheme.description: ASCII text would not need converting to new codes

questions.prompt: A program reads the character 7 typed by a user and adds 1 to its ASCII code. What character results, and why is this not 8 as a number?
options: The character 1, because only the added value is kept
The number 8, because adding to a code adds to its decimal value
The character 8, because the digits run in sequence from 48
Nothing valid, because codes cannot be added to
questions.solution: The character 7 has code **55**, and 55 + 1 = 56, which is the character **8** — because the digit characters run in sequence from 48. It looks like arithmetic on the number but it is not: the program moved one place along the **character** group. Genuine arithmetic needs the character converted to a number first.

markScheme.description: the character 8, as digits run in sequence

questions.prompt: How many bits are needed to store the word "Cat" in 7-bit ASCII?
questions.solution: Three characters at 7 bits each: $3 \times 7 = $ **21** bits. Note that the capital and the lower case letters take the same space — the case affects the code, not the size.

questions.prompt: Why can character codes be worked out from a single known code, such as A = 65?
options: Codes are grouped and run in sequence within each group
Every code is a multiple of the first code in its group
All character sets use the same codes for every character
Codes are assigned randomly but stored in a lookup table
questions.solution: The specification states that codes are **grouped and run in sequence**. Because the capitals occupy consecutive codes from 65, every other capital can be calculated once one is known — and the same holds for lower case and for digits.

markScheme.description: codes are grouped and run in sequence

questions.prompt: Two computers exchange a text file and one displays nonsense. What does this suggest?
options: The file was too large to transfer completely
They are interpreting the codes with different character sets
One computer stores text in decimal rather than binary
Character codes change when a file is copied
questions.solution: The bits arrive unchanged; what differs is the **agreement about what they mean**. If the two machines use different character sets, the same code stands for a different character on each. This was a real and constant problem before Unicode, and avoiding it is exactly why a single worldwide standard matters.

questions.prompt: Explain what a character set is, describe how ASCII represents characters, and explain how a code can be worked out from a known one.
questions.solution:
A **character set** is an agreed list of the characters a system can use, in which each character is paired with a **unique binary code**. One is needed because a computer stores everything as binary, so without an agreement about which pattern stands for which character a stored file would be meaningless — and meaningless in a **different** way on every machine that opened it.

It is worth being clear that a "character" is more than a letter. Digits, punctuation, the space and **control characters** such as carriage return all have codes of their own.

**ASCII** is a **7-bit** character set. Seven bits give $2^7 = $ **128** different patterns, so ASCII has **128** characters with codes numbered **0 to 127**. That is enough for the English alphabet in both cases, the ten digits, punctuation and the control characters, and nothing more — no accented letters, no other alphabets, no mathematical symbols.

**Codes are grouped, and each group runs in sequence.** The capital letters occupy consecutive codes beginning at **A = 65**, the lower case letters beginning at **a = 97**, and the digit characters beginning at **0 = 48**.

This is what allows a code to be worked out from a known one. To find the code for **F**, note that F is the 6th letter of the alphabet and therefore **5** places along from A, **counting from 0**. So its code is $65 + 5 = \mathbf{70}$. Counting from 1 instead would give 71, and that off-by-one is an easy slip.

The same method works backwards. A character with code 84 is $84 - 65 = 19$ places on from A, which makes it the 20th capital letter, **T**.

Two details follow from the grouping. Upper and lower case differ by exactly **32** for every letter, since $97 - 65 = 32$, so changing case is a matter of adding or subtracting 32. And the **digit characters are not the values they show**: the character `'7'` has the code $48 + 7 = \mathbf{55}$, not 7. This is why a program must convert a typed digit before doing arithmetic with it.

questions.prompt: Compare ASCII and Unicode. Explain why Unicode was needed, its advantages, and what it costs.
questions.solution:
**ASCII** is a 7-bit character set, which gives it $2^7 = $ **128** characters with codes from 0 to 127. That was designed for English on American equipment and it covers that job exactly: both cases of the alphabet, the ten digits, punctuation and control characters.

**The limitation is that 128 is a very small number.** There is no room in ASCII for accented letters such as é, for Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew, Chinese or Japanese, or for mathematical symbols, currency signs and emoji. As computers spread beyond English-speaking countries this became untenable. Various incompatible extensions of ASCII appeared, and text moved between countries frequently arrived as nonsense — the bits were unchanged, but the two machines disagreed about what they meant.

**Unicode's purpose** is to solve that properly: to give **every character in every writing system** a single unique code. It achieves this by using **more bits per character** than ASCII, which buys room for well over a hundred thousand characters.

**Its advantages** follow from that. It can represent **all alphabets**, not just English. Text in **any language** can be stored and exchanged, and several languages can appear in one document. Because it is a **single worldwide standard**, a file displays the same way wherever it is opened, which removes the whole class of problem described above.

**Its disadvantage is size.** More bits per character means **larger files** for the same text. For plain English — which ASCII already handled — Unicode takes more space for no visible gain. That is the genuine cost, and a comparison that does not mention it is incomplete. A common mistake is to claim Unicode produces *smaller* files, which has the trade-off exactly backwards.

**The compatibility point is what made adoption possible.** The first **128** Unicode codes are **identical** to ASCII's. Unicode could have renumbered everything and been tidier, but keeping those codes meant every ASCII character kept the same code in Unicode, so ASCII text did not need renumbering. Designing for the text that already existed, rather than only for the problem in hand, made the move to Unicode easier.

The specification does not require any knowledge of UTF-8, UTF-16 or other versions of Unicode.

questions.prompt: In ASCII the code for a is 97, and the lower case letters run in sequence. Which character has the code 104?
options: H
h
g
i
questions.solution: $104 - 97 = 7$, so it is 7 places on from a. Counting a as 0 places along, that is the 8th letter, lower case **h**. Taking 7 as the 7th letter gives g, the off-by-one; capital H has the code 72, which is 32 less.

questions.prompt: In ASCII the character 0 has the code 48, and the digit characters run in sequence. A character is stored as the 7-bit binary code 0110100. Which character is it?
questions.solution: Convert the binary first: `0110100` has 1s under 32, 16 and 4, so the code is $32 + 16 + 4 = 52$. Then $52 - 48 = 4$, so it is 4 places on from the character 0: the character **4**. It is the character 4, stored as code 52, not the number 52.

questions.prompt:
Part of the ASCII table is shown. The codes run in sequence within each group.

| Character | Code |
| --- | --- |
| A | 65 |
| a | 97 |

Which word is stored as the codes 83, 116, 97, 114?
options: star
Tubs
STAR
Star
questions.solution: 83 is $83 - 65 = 18$ places on from A, the 19th capital letter, **S**. 116 is $116 - 97 = 19$ places on from a, **t**. 97 is **a**, and 114 is 17 places on from a, **r**. So the word is **Star**, with a capital S. *star* and *STAR* each have a different code for at least one letter, and *Tubs* is every code read one place too far.

examTechnique.body:
Count places from **0**: A is 65 and is 0 places along, so F is $65 + 5 = 70$. Check the **case** first — capitals start at 65, lower case at 97, a gap of **32**.

Keep the **character** apart from the **value**: `'7'` is 55. For Unicode, give the purpose as **covering every writing system**, and admit the cost — **larger files**.

Giving Unicode's purpose as "it is bigger".
Forgetting that the space and punctuation have codes.
Writing about UTF-8 or UTF-16, which are not required.

examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer counts from **0** and checks the **case** before working anything out, so it never lands 32 away from the right code. It keeps the **character** `'7'` (code 55) distinct from the **number** 7, and can say why that matters for a program reading input. On Unicode it gives the purpose as **a code for every writing system**, names the cost — **more bits, larger files** — and makes the point that is easy to miss: the first **128** codes are identical to ASCII, so ASCII text keeps its codes and did not need renumbering.
